9370:
To understand this idiom, you first need to know how a courtroom works.

In a legal trial, a jury is a group of ordinary citizens (usually 12 people) who listen to all the evidence in a case and then decide whether someone is guilty or innocent. After hearing everything, the jury leaves the courtroom and goes into a private room to discuss and reach a decision. This is called jury deliberation.

While the jury is away in that private room, nobody knows the verdict yet. The judge doesn't know. The lawyers don't know. The public doesn't know. Everyone is simply waiting. The matter is unresolved and uncertain.

So when someone says "the jury is still out," they are picturing that moment — the jury has not come back yet, and no decision has been made.
The Idiomatic Meaning (What It Actually Means in Everyday Life)

When used as an idiom, "the jury is still out" means:

A final decision, conclusion, or judgment has not yet been reached. The matter is still uncertain, and people are still debating or waiting for more information.

It has nothing to do with an actual courtroom. You use it to talk about any situation in life where something is still undecided, unproven, or unclear.

Think of it this way:

  • Jury = the people (or the world, or experts, or time itself) who will eventually decide something
  • Still out = they haven't come back with a verdict yet
  • Together = we don't know the answer yet; it's too early to say

Example 1:

"Scientists have been studying this new diet for years, but the jury is still out on whether it actually works long-term."

👉 This means scientists haven't reached a definitive conclusion yet. More research and evidence is needed before anyone can say for certain.

Example 2:

"He's only been the new manager for two weeks. The jury is still out on whether he's the right person for the job."

👉 It's too early to judge whether the manager is good or bad. People are watching and waiting before forming a solid opinion.

Example 3:

"I tried the new restaurant downtown. The food was okay, but the jury's still out — I need to go a couple more times before I decide if I love it."

👉 The speaker hasn't made up their mind yet. They need more experience before reaching a conclusion.

Example 4:

"The jury is still out on whether electric cars are truly better for the environment when you consider the full manufacturing process."

👉 Experts and researchers are still debating this. No definitive, universally agreed-upon answer exists yet.
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This phrase carries a tone of honest uncertainty. It signals that:

  • You are open-minded and not rushing to judge.
  • You acknowledge that not enough information or time has passed to make a fair decision.
  • You are intellectually honest — you're not pretending to know something you don't.

It is generally a neutral to slightly cautious phrase. It doesn't mean something is bad. It just means: "We don't know yet."

The phrase is often slightly shortened or tweaked in casual speech. All of these mean the same thing:

  • "The jury's still out on that." (most common casual form)
  • "The jury is out on whether..."
  • "The jury's out."
  • "The jury is still out on this one."

You might also hear the opposite phrase: "The jury is in" or "The jury has spoken" — meaning a decision HAS been made, and the matter is settled.

You'll hear or read this phrase in many different contexts:

  • Science and medicine: When research is ongoing and results are not yet conclusive.
  • Business and leadership: When a new hire, product, or strategy hasn't proven itself yet.
  • Politics: When a policy's effectiveness is still being observed.
  • Everyday opinions: When someone personally hasn't made up their mind about something (a movie, a restaurant, a person, etc.).

Avoid using it when a conclusion is already clear and widely accepted. For example, it would be strange (and factually wrong) to say:

❌ "The jury is still out on whether the Earth is round."

That's already settled. The idiom is for genuinely open, unresolved questions — not questions that have clear answers.
"The jury is still out" = We don't have a final answer yet. It's too early to say. The matter is still being decided.

Picture a courtroom frozen in time — the judge is sitting there, the lawyers are nervously tapping their pens, and the seats where the jury sits are empty. Everyone is waiting. No verdict. No closure. No answer.

That frozen, waiting feeling — that's exactly what this idiom means.
9371:
Jury-rigged describes something that has been quickly put together or repaired using whatever materials happen to be available at the time, because the proper parts, tools, or resources aren't on hand.

The result works — or works well enough — but it's improvised, rough, and almost always temporary. It was not built or fixed the right way; it was fixed the available way.

Think of it this way: imagine you're camping and the leg of your chair snaps. You don't have glue, screws, or a spare chair. So you find a sturdy stick, press it against the broken leg, and wrap the whole thing tightly with shoelaces. You sit down, and it holds. That chair is now jury-rigged.

It solves the problem. It functions. But anyone looking at it can tell immediately that this is not how a chair is supposed to be built. It's a clever workaround, not a proper fix.

A jury-rigged thing typically has all four of these qualities:

  1. Improvised — made from whatever was nearby, not the correct parts
  2. Functional — it actually works, at least for now
  3. Visibly rough — it looks patched together, not clean or professional
  4. Temporary (in spirit) — it was never meant to be a lasting solution

This last point is important. Jury-rigged things can end up lasting a long time in practice, but the intention was always just to get by until a proper solution was possible.
The Tone: Is It a Compliment or a Criticism?

Both, depending on context — and this is one of the most interesting things about this word.

  • When someone is in a tough situation and makes something work with limited resources, calling their solution "jury-rigged" can carry a tone of admiration. It suggests cleverness, quick thinking, and resourcefulness.

    "With no spare parts and a storm approaching, the sailor jury-rigged the broken mast using rope and planks — and it held through the night."

    Here, "jury-rigged" sounds almost heroic.

  • But in everyday life, when someone takes a shortcut on something that deserved a proper fix, "jury-rigged" can carry a tone of mild criticism or even amusement.

    "The whole electrical system in that old house is jury-rigged — wires taped together, fuses replaced with pennies. It's a miracle it still works."

    Here, it sounds careless and risky.

So the word itself is neutral — it simply describes how something was put together. The judgment depends on whether the improvisation was necessary and clever, or lazy and reckless.

• "They couldn't afford a proper studio, so they built a jury-rigged recording booth using blankets hung from the ceiling and foam egg cartons on the walls."
  • "His jury-rigged phone stand — a stack of books with a binder clip on top — somehow worked perfectly for video calls."
  • "The spacecraft had a jury-rigged CO₂ filter, assembled from duct tape and spare parts, that kept the crew alive long enough to return home." (This is loosely based on the real Apollo 13 mission.)
  • "Don't touch that jury-rigged shelf — it's just a plank resting on two stacks of bricks."

In every case, notice: something is functioning, but it was assembled in a makeshift, unpolished way.
A Very Common Mix-Up: "Jury-Rigged" vs. "Jerry-Rigged" vs. "Jerry-Built"

Since you want to know everything about this word, you need to know about its two close relatives, because people confuse all three constantly — even native speakers.

Jury-riggedImprovised and makeshift, but functional. The focus is on clever improvisation. ✅ Standard, correct usage.
Jerry-riggedThis is widely used in spoken American English and means the same thing as jury-rigged. Many people use it without knowing it. Strictly speaking, it is an informal, corrupted blend of "jury-rigged" and "jerry-built" (see below), but it's so common that most dictionaries now accept it as a valid variant.
Jerry-builtBuilt cheaply, shoddily, and poorly — but without the sense of improvisation or cleverness. A jerry-built house was not made from random parts in an emergency; it was simply constructed badly, probably to save money. This word is a pure criticism with no admiring angle at all.

The easiest way to keep them straight:

  • Jury-rigged → improvised fix, often under pressure, often resourceful
  • Jerry-built → just plain badly made, cheaply and sloppily
The Bigger Picture: What Kind of Word Is It?

As an adjective, "jury-rigged" always modifies a noun — it describes the thing that was improvised.

  • A jury-rigged antenna
  • A jury-rigged solution
  • A jury-rigged engine repair

You can also find it used after a linking verb:

  • "The whole setup was jury-rigged."
  • "The repairs looked jury-rigged."

It's common in both spoken and written English, and it works across many registers — from casual conversation to journalism to technical writing.

Jury-rigged = put together quickly and roughly with whatever was available, in a way that works but is clearly improvised and not done properly.

That's the whole word. Resourceful, rough, functional, and temporary — all at once.
9372:
"Just deserts" means getting exactly what you deserve — usually a punishment that fits a wrongdoing.

When someone does something bad and then suffers a fitting consequence for it, we say they got their "just deserts." The phrase carries a strong sense of fairness and justice — the idea that the universe balanced the scales correctly.

The corrupt politician was finally sent to prison. He got his just deserts.

The key feeling behind the phrase is satisfaction — a sense that of course this happened, because it was the right and fair outcome.

The Word "Just"

Here, "just" does not mean "only" or "simply" (as in, "I just want a glass of water"). Instead, it means fair, morally right, and appropriate. Think of a "just" judge — one who gives rulings that are fair and deserved.

The Word "Deserts"

This is where almost everyone gets confused, so pay very close attention.

The word "deserts" here is an old, archaic noun that most people don't use anymore in everyday English. It comes from the old French word deservir, meaning "to deserve." So "deserts" (used as a noun) simply meant "that which a person deserves."

This meaning of the word is essentially dead in modern English — it only survives inside this one idiom. That's why it confuses people so much. If you saw the word "deserts" anywhere else today, you'd think of either the sandy Sahara or something sweet after dinner. But inside this phrase, it means something completely different.

This idiom has one of the most common spelling mistakes in the English language. There are three words that look or sound similar, and it's critical to know the difference:

1. Desert (DEZ-ert) — The dry, sandy landscape. The Sahara is a desert.

2. Deserts (dih-ZERTS) — The correct word in this idiom. An archaic noun meaning "what one deserves." He got his just deserts.

3. Desserts (dih-ZERTS) — The sweet food you eat after a meal. She ordered chocolate cake for dessert.

Here is the trap: "deserts" (the idiom word) and "desserts" (the sweet food) are pronounced identically. Both sound like dih-ZERTS. But they are spelled differently, and they mean completely different things.

Because they sound the same, millions of people write "just desserts" — as if someone is getting a fair helping of cake. This is wrong. The correct spelling is always "just deserts" — one "s" in the middle, not two.

Also notice: the "desert" in this idiom is not pronounced like the sandy landscape (DEZ-ert, with the stress on the first syllable). It is pronounced like the sweet food — dih-ZERTS, with the stress on the second syllable. Same sound, different spelling, totally different meaning. English can be cruel like that.

Since the spelling trips everyone up, here's a trick to remember it:

"Just deserts" is about what you deserve. Both "deserve" and "deserts" start with D-E-S-E-R. Lock that connection in your mind.

If you remember that "deserts" in this phrase is a cousin of the word "deserve," you'll never misspell it as "desserts" again.

While the phrase technically can apply to positive outcomes (a hero getting rewarded, for example), in real-world usage it is almost always used for negative, punishing outcomes. It carries a tone of moral satisfaction — like justice being served cold and correctly.

It often implies that the person waited a while for this consequence, or that the consequence is particularly fitting for what they did. It's not neutral — it has a slightly dramatic, weighty feel to it.

• After years of cheating his business partners, he lost everything. It was his just deserts.
  • The bully finally got his just deserts when the school expelled him.
  • Many felt the reckless driver got his just deserts when his license was permanently revoked.
  • She worked hard her entire career and finally got promoted — you could argue that was her just deserts too. (positive use, less common)

ComponentDetail
  • Meaning: Receiving the punishment or reward you truly deserve, especially a fitting punishment.
  • "Just" means fair and morally right.
  • "Deserts" is an old noun meaning "what one deserves" — not the sandy landscape, not the sweet food.
  • Correct spelling: just deserts (one "s" in the middle).
  • Wrong spelling: just desserts — very common mistake, always incorrect.
  • Pronunciation of "deserts" here: dih-ZERTS — like the sweet food, not like the Sahara.
  • Tone: Usually used with moral satisfaction when a wrongdoer faces fitting consequences.

That is everything you will ever need to know about "just deserts." The meaning is simple; the spelling is the only thing that requires your attention — and now you know exactly why it trips people up and how to get it right every single time.
9373:
When you say something is "just what the doctor ordered," you mean it is exactly what was needed — perfectly suited to solve a problem, satisfy a need, or improve a situation.

It expresses that something arrived at the right time, in the right form, and worked out perfectly. There is a sense of relief and satisfaction in the phrase — like, "Yes! That's it. That's exactly what I needed."
Where It Comes From

The image behind this idiom is simple: imagine you are sick and you go to a doctor. The doctor examines you and prescribes the one medicine that will cure you. That medicine is exactly what was needed — not too strong, not too weak, not the wrong type. It is the precise remedy for your problem.

Over time, people began using this medical image as a metaphor in everyday life — not just for medicines, but for anything that feels like the perfect solution or the perfect comfort in a moment of need.

The idiom has been in common use in English since at least the early 20th century and is widely used in both American and British English.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

• "Just" — here means exactly or precisely, not merely. It emphasises how perfectly something fits the situation.
  • "What the doctor ordered" — what the doctor prescribed, i.e., the specific remedy for your condition.

Put together: This is precisely the remedy my situation needed.
Examples in Real Life

Example 1 — After a tiring day:

"I've been on my feet all day. This hot cup of tea is just what the doctor ordered."

(Meaning: The tea is the perfect thing to relax and refresh me right now.)

Example 2 — After bad news:

"I was feeling so low after the rejection. That phone call from my best friend was just what the doctor ordered."

(Meaning: The phone call was exactly the comfort and encouragement I needed.)

Example 3 — At work:

"The team was losing motivation. The manager's encouraging speech was just what the doctor ordered."

(Meaning: The speech perfectly addressed the team's need for motivation.)

Example 4 — With food or drinks:

"It's a freezing evening. A bowl of hot soup would be just what the doctor ordered."

(Meaning: Hot soup is the ideal thing for this cold weather.)

Example 5 — After a difficult situation:

"We had a stressful week. That weekend trip to the mountains was just what the doctor ordered."

(Meaning: The trip was the perfect cure for the stress.)
The Feeling Behind the Idiom

This idiom carries a warm, positive, and satisfied tone. When you use it, you are not just saying something is "good" — you are saying it is perfectly timed and perfectly suited to what was needed. There is a subtle sense of relief in it, almost like a sigh: "Ah, exactly what I needed."

It often implies that you were in some kind of discomfort — physical tiredness, emotional stress, boredom, hunger, cold — and this particular thing came along and resolved it beautifully.
When Can You Use It?

You can use this idiom in many contexts:

  • Physical comfort (food, drink, rest, warmth, sleep)
  • Emotional comfort (a kind word, a hug, a conversation with a friend)
  • Professional situations (a solution to a problem, a boost of morale, a helpful resource)
  • Entertainment and leisure (a movie, a holiday, a walk)

Essentially, any time something fits a need perfectly, this idiom works.
Tone and Register

This is a casual, informal expression. It suits everyday conversation, friendly writing, and informal speech. You would not typically use it in a formal academic essay or a serious legal document. However, it is perfectly appropriate in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Informal emails and messages
  • Newspaper columns and casual journalism
  • Storytelling and fiction
What This Idiom Is NOT Saying

It is important to note what this phrase does not mean:

  • It does not mean a literal doctor prescribed something.
  • It does not suggest that the situation was medically serious.
  • It does not mean something is merely "good" — it means something is specifically and perfectly suited to the moment.

The medical reference is purely metaphorical.
A Common Variation

You will sometimes hear the phrase with a slight variation:

"That's just what the doctor ordered!"

This is the most common version — using "that's" to point to a specific thing that just happened or was just received. Both forms mean the same thing.
How to Remember It

Think of it this way:

A doctor's prescription is not random. It is carefully chosen for your specific problem, at this specific moment. When you say something is "just what the doctor ordered," you are saying it fits your situation with that same kind of precision — like it was chosen especially for you.
Quick Summary

MeaningExactly what was needed; a perfect solution or comfort for a situation
ToneWarm, positive, satisfied, relieved
RegisterInformal and everyday
OriginMetaphor from medical prescriptions
Used forPhysical comfort, emotional support, practical solutions, leisure

In short: if something comes along and solves your problem or makes you feel better in exactly the right way, it is just what the doctor ordered. The phrase celebrates that perfect match between a need and what fulfils it.
9374:
Justifiable describes something — an action, decision, feeling, or belief — that can be proven to be right, reasonable, or acceptable using valid, logical reasons.

If something is justifiable, it means that when someone questions it or challenges it, you are able to defend it with solid reasons, and most reasonable people would agree: "Yes, given the circumstances, that makes sense."

Think of it this way:

To justify something = to give good enough reasons to show it was right or acceptable.
Justifiable = something for which such good reasons exist.

So the word essentially answers the question: "Can this be defended with valid reasoning?" If the answer is yes — it is justifiable.
The Heart of the Word: "Can It Be Defended?"

The most important thing to understand about "justifiable" is that it is about the existence of a valid defense or reason — not just any defense, but one that holds up under scrutiny.

Imagine you arrive late to work. Your boss asks why. You say:

  • "I overslept because I stayed up watching TV." → Not justifiable. There is no strong reason here.
  • "There was a car accident on the highway, and traffic was completely blocked." → Justifiable. The reason is real, beyond your control, and anyone would understand.

The late arrival in the second case is justifiable because it can be reasonably explained and defended.

For something to be called justifiable, the reasons behind it usually need to pass a kind of "reasonable person test" — meaning: would a sensible, fair-minded person look at the situation and agree that the action or feeling made sense?

The reasons need to be:

Logical — They make rational sense, not just emotional excuses.
Proportionate — The action or response fits the scale of the situation.
Understandable in context — The circumstances make the action or feeling reasonable.

If all three hold up, something is likely justifiable. If any of these are weak or missing, people may call it unjustifiable — meaning it cannot be reasonably defended.

1. Justifiable ≠ Perfect or Ideal

Something can be justifiable without being the best possible choice. It simply means the reasoning behind it is strong enough to make it acceptable or defensible — not necessarily flawless.

For example: A company cutting staff during a financial crisis may be justifiable (the business is losing money and may collapse otherwise), even if it's not the most desirable outcome.

2. Context Is Everything

Whether something is justifiable depends heavily on the situation. The same action can be justifiable in one context and completely unjustifiable in another.

Hitting someone is generally not justifiable. But hitting someone who is attacking you — to defend yourself — may be entirely justifiable, because the context (self-defense) provides strong, valid reasons.

3. Justifiable Often Has a Moral or Ethical Dimension

The word is frequently used when judging whether something should have been done — it carries a built-in ethical weight. When someone asks "Was it justifiable?", they are usually asking: "Was it morally or logically acceptable, given the circumstances?"

4. Degree Matters

Justifiability is not always black and white. Something can be:

  • Clearly / fully justifiable — Most reasonable people agree it was right or acceptable.
  • Arguably / barely justifiable — There are some valid reasons, but it is debatable.
  • Wholly unjustifiable — There are no valid reasons; it simply cannot be defended.
Common Situations Where the Word Is Used

Justifiable anger / outrage
Anger that makes complete sense given what happened. If someone cheats you, your anger is justifiable — you have every good reason to feel it.

Justifiable concern / worry
Worry that is reasonable because there are real, genuine reasons to be worried. If a doctor tells you a surgery carries risks, your concern is justifiable.

Justifiable response / reaction
A reaction that appropriately matches what triggered it. If someone insults you publicly, a firm response would be considered justifiable.

Justifiable decision / choice
A decision that can be logically defended with solid reasoning, even if not everyone agrees with the outcome.

Justifiable homicide (legal and formal context)
This is a specific legal term meaning the act of killing someone was legally acceptable — most commonly in cases of genuine self-defense — where there were valid, recognized reasons under the law.

Justifiable expense / cost
Spending that can be reasonably defended as necessary or appropriate given the situation.

"His frustration with the delays was completely justifiable — he had been waiting for three hours."
→ His frustration made perfect sense; anyone would understand it.

"The government argued that the emergency restrictions were justifiable given the severity of the crisis."
→ The restrictions could be logically defended based on the circumstances.

"She refused to accept that his behavior was justifiable under any circumstances."
→ She believed there were no valid reasons that could make his behavior acceptable.

"The expense was justifiable because it prevented a much larger financial loss later."
→ The spending made logical sense and could be defended with sound reasoning.

"It is hard to say whether his anger is truly justifiable, or whether he is overreacting."
→ Whether his anger is reasonable and defensible is open to debate.

Knowing the whole family of words helps you understand "justifiable" even more deeply:

Justify (verb) — to give valid reasons that prove something is right or acceptable. "He struggled to justify his decision."

Justified (adjective) — very similar to justifiable, but with a subtle difference: "justified" means the reasons have already been accepted and recognized, while "justifiable" means the reasons exist and can be shown. In practice, they are often used interchangeably.

Justification (noun) — the actual reason or explanation given to defend something. "There is no justification for that kind of behavior."

Unjustifiable (adjective) — the direct opposite: something for which no valid defense or reason exists; completely indefensible. "The attack on civilians was wholly unjustifiable."

Justifiably (adverb) — in a justifiable manner; with good reason. "She was justifiably upset."

Whenever you are unsure whether to use "justifiable," ask yourself:

"Could a fair, reasonable person look at this situation and agree that there were solid, logical reasons for this action / feeling / decision?"

If yes → it is justifiable.
If no → it is unjustifiable.

Justifiable means able to be shown as right, reasonable, or acceptable based on valid reasons — it describes something that can be logically and fairly defended when questioned, given the circumstances in which it occurred.
9375:
A justification is a reason — or a set of reasons — given to show that something is right, fair, acceptable, or necessary. It is the act of defending something, and the word refers to the defense itself.

Think of it this way: you arrive an hour late to a meeting. Your boss asks why. You say, "There was a serious accident on the highway and the road was completely blocked." That explanation is your justification. You're not just describing what happened — you're arguing that your lateness was understandable and acceptable given the circumstances.

A justification, at its core, answers the question: "Why was this okay, necessary, or right?"

This is crucial: a justification doesn't merely explain what happened — it makes a case that what happened was reasonable or acceptable. That's what separates it from a plain description.

"I was late because I overslept" is a description of what happened. "I was late because I was helping a woman who had collapsed on the street" is a justification — it actively argues that your behavior was acceptable, even admirable.

These two words are commonly confused, but they mean something quite different:

An excuse admits that something was wrong but tries to reduce your blame. "I know I shouldn't have shouted, but I was under tremendous stress."

A justification argues that what you did was not wrong at all — that it was the right or acceptable thing to do. "I had every right to shout, because he was about to hurt someone."

When you give a justification, you are not saying "I was wrong, please forgive me." You are saying "What I did was right — and here is why."

A justification can be strong (valid) or weak (flawed, even dishonest).

A valid justification genuinely demonstrates why something was acceptable. A weak or invalid justification fails to do this — it may be illogical, based on false information, or simply not compelling enough.

"I took the food because my children were starving and there was no other way" is widely regarded as a strong justification. "I took it because I felt like it" is no justification at all.

This is why people say "That's no justification!" — meaning: your reason doesn't actually make your behavior acceptable.

In everyday speech, "justification" is used broadly to mean any sound reason behind an action, belief, or decision. A few examples:

  • "There is no justification for cruelty." — No reason makes cruelty acceptable.
  • "Can you give me a justification for this decision?" — Explain to me why this decision is the right one.
  • "She felt her anger was completely justified." — She believed her anger was a fair, reasonable response.

Notice that the word almost always carries a moral undertone. It implies that someone has questioned whether something was right — and the justification is the answer to that challenge.

In legal contexts, justification has a precise technical meaning: a legally recognized reason that makes an otherwise unlawful act lawful.

Killing someone is normally a serious crime. But if you killed someone in genuine self-defense — because they were about to kill you and you had absolutely no other option — the law may recognize self-defense as a justification. The act itself (killing) would normally be criminal, but the justification (protecting your life) makes it legally permissible.

This is different from a legal excuse. A legal excuse (such as insanity) says "the person did something wrong but should not be punished." A legal justification says "the person didn't actually do anything wrong, given the circumstances — the act itself was permissible."

In philosophy, justification refers to having adequate evidence or sound reasoning to support a belief — to show that you have proper grounds for believing something to be true.

For example: if you believe the Earth is round because of scientific evidence, your belief is justified. If you believe the Earth is flat because you dreamed it, your belief is not justified — your reasons are insufficient.

Philosophers propose a classic formula: knowledge = justified true belief. You truly "know" something only if (a) it is actually true, (b) you believe it, and (c) you have justification for believing it. Without justification, you might hold a true belief purely by lucky guess — but that doesn't count as real knowledge.

In Christian theology — especially in Protestant traditions — "justification" carries a very specific and profound meaning: it is the act by which God declares a sinful person righteous and forgiven in His sight.

The idea is that humans are sinful and therefore guilty before God, but through faith in Jesus Christ, God "justifies" them — He declares them not guilty, acquitted, and accepted. This was one of the central teachings of Martin Luther and the Protestant Reformation.

In this theological sense, justification is not something a person earns through good deeds. It is understood as a gift of God's grace. Catholic theology holds a related but distinct view — seeing justification more as an ongoing process of becoming righteous, rather than purely being declared righteous.

This is a completely unrelated but common use of the word, found in printing, publishing, and word processing.

In typography, "justification" means aligning text so that every line stretches from the left margin to the right margin, creating clean, even edges on both sides of a page. You see this constantly in books, newspapers, and formal documents. When text is "fully justified," no line ends raggedly — every line is neatly aligned on both sides.

You have almost certainly seen justified text your whole life without knowing this word for it.

Across all its meanings, a justification is fundamentally about showing that something meets a required standard — moral, legal, intellectual, or divine.

In everyday life, it's a reason that makes an action acceptable. In law, it's what makes an otherwise unlawful act lawful. In philosophy, it's the evidence that makes a belief legitimate. In theology, it's God's declaration of a person's righteousness. In typography, it's even text alignment meeting a visual standard.

The word always implies that something has been (or could be) questioned — and the justification is the answer that says: "This was right. Here is why."
9376:
To justify something means to show that it is right, reasonable, or acceptable — usually by giving reasons or evidence.

When you justify something, you are essentially saying: "Here is why this is okay. Here is why this makes sense." You are defending or explaining something so that others (or even yourself) can accept it as fair or valid.
The Two Main Ways "Justify" Is Used

1. A person justifies something

Here, a person gives reasons to defend or explain an action, decision, belief, or behaviour.

  • She justified her absence by saying she was ill.
  • He struggled to justify why he had spent so much money.
  • The manager justified the new policy to the team.

Notice the pattern: someone justifies [something] by [giving a reason]. The "by" part is optional — sometimes you simply say someone justified their choice, and the reason is understood from context.

2. A thing justifies something else

Here, the subject is not a person but a thing — a result, a situation, a fact. The idea is that this thing is reason enough for something else to happen.

  • The excellent results justify the effort we put in. (= The results are good enough to make the effort worthwhile.)
  • Nothing can justify cruelty. (= No reason is good enough to make cruelty acceptable.)
  • The high cost does not justify the poor quality.

This is a very important use. It asks the question: Is this good enough a reason? When something justifies something else, it means it provides sufficient grounds — a strong enough reason — for that thing.
The Famous Phrase: "Does the end justify the means?"

This is one of the most well-known expressions using this word.

"The end" = the final goal or result you want to achieve.
"The means" = the actions or methods you use to get there.

The question asks: If the final outcome is good, does that make it okay to use harmful or unfair methods to reach it?

For example: Is it okay to lie to protect someone you love? The "end" (protecting them) might be good, but the "means" (lying) might be wrong. This question has no simple answer, which is why it has been debated by thinkers for centuries.

When someone tells you to justify yourself, they are asking you to explain and defend your actions to them. It often carries a slightly demanding or confrontational tone — the person wants to know why you did what you did and whether it was acceptable.

  • "You were two hours late. Can you justify yourself?"

"Justify" is not a neutral word. It carries a specific flavour: there is something that needs defending. You don't usually justify things that are obviously fine. When someone says "I can justify this," there is an implied sense that someone might question it, and the speaker is prepared to defend it.

Compare:

  • "I explained my plan." → neutral; just sharing information.
  • "I justified my plan." → suggests the plan was questioned or could be doubted, and I gave reasons to show it was sound.

This is why "justify" often appears in serious, formal, or critical contexts — in law (justifying an action in court), in ethics (justifying a moral choice), in business (justifying a budget), or in everyday disagreements.

The adjective forms are very common and useful.

  • Justified = having a good enough reason; fair and reasonable.
    • His anger was completely justified. (= His anger made sense; there was a real reason for it.)
    • a justified concern (= a concern that is reasonable, not baseless)
  • Unjustified = without good reason; unfair; not warranted.
    • The attack was unjustified. (= There was no valid reason for it.)
    • unjustified criticism (= criticism that is unfair or baseless)

A justification is the reason or explanation you give to justify something. It is the content of your defense.

  • What is your justification for this decision? (= What reasons do you have?)
  • There is no justification for such behaviour. (= No reason makes it acceptable.)
  • He offered several justifications, but none were convincing.
The Typography Meaning (a separate, specific use)

In word processing and printing, "justify" has a technical meaning: to align text so that both the left and right edges form straight, even lines. This is done by automatically adjusting the spaces between words.

  • Left-justified = text is aligned to the left margin (this is the default in most documents).
  • Right-justified = text is aligned to the right margin.
  • Fully justified (or simply "justified") = text is stretched so both the left AND right margins are perfectly straight, like in most newspapers and books.

When you see a news article where every line ends perfectly at the same point on the right side, that text has been justified. You are essentially making each line fit a defined space evenly.
Summary of All Meanings at a Glance

UseWhat it means

To justify means to give good enough reasons to show that something is right, fair, or acceptable. A person can justify their actions (defend them with reasons). A thing or situation can justify something else (be a sufficient reason for it). The adjective justified means something was fair and had good grounds; unjustified means it did not. The noun justification is the reason itself. And in typography, to justify text means to align it so both margins are even.

The word always circles back to the same central question: Is there a good enough reason for this?
9377:
When something juts, it sticks out sharply and noticeably from a surface or a line, extending into the space around it. Think of it as something "pushing itself forward" or "poking outward" in a way that is sudden, definite, and easy to notice.

The key feeling of this word is sharpness and abruptness. It is not a soft, gentle curve outward — it is a bold, clear, definite projection.

Imagine you are standing at the edge of the sea, looking at a coastline. The coastline runs roughly in a line — but then, suddenly, a large mass of rock pushes forward into the water, well beyond the rest of the coast. That rock juts out into the sea.

Or imagine a brick wall. All the bricks sit flat and even — but one brick has come slightly loose and its edge is pushing outward. That brick juts out from the wall.

The thing doing the "jutting" always breaks away from the surrounding surface or line and enters the space beyond it.
How It Is Used in Sentences

"Jut" almost always appears with the word "out" — you will see "jut out" far more often than "jut" alone. Sometimes you will also see it with "into", "over", or "above", depending on which direction the thing is pointing.

Here are examples across different situations:

Landscape and nature:

  • The rocky cliff juts out over the ocean far below.
  • A narrow strip of land juts into the lake, almost like a natural pier.
  • A sharp peak juts above the surrounding mountain range.

Buildings and structures:

  • A small balcony juts out from the side of the building.
  • Old wooden beams jut out from the ceiling of the ancient barn.
  • The corner of the metal shelf juts out dangerously into the hallway.

Objects:

  • Be careful — a nail juts out from that old floorboard.
  • The door handle juts out just enough to catch on your coat as you walk by.

The human body:

  • His strong jaw juts forward when he is being stubborn or determined.
  • Her cheekbones jut out sharply, giving her face a striking look.
  • The man's elbow jutted out as he rested his arm on the table.

This is what separates "jut" from simple words like "stick out." While both mean roughly the same thing, "jut" carries a stronger sense of sharpness, angularity, and definiteness. When something "juts," it does so in a way that is bold and clearly visible — it commands your attention because it breaks so noticeably from everything around it.

A gentle, soft curve outward — like a pillow bulging slightly — would not be described as "jutting." But a rocky ledge, a sharp chin, a pointed tower, a protruding beam — these "jut," because they extend in a way that is firm, sudden, and pronounced.

Something can jut in several directions:

  • Outward — away from a surface (most common use)
  • Forward — ahead of the surrounding line (especially for jaws, chins, foreheads)
  • Upward — rising above the surrounding level (a peak jutting above the clouds)
  • Into something — extending into a body of space (a peninsula jutting into the sea)
A Simple One-Line Definition to Remember

To jut means to extend sharply and noticeably outward beyond the surrounding surface or line.

Whenever you see it, ask yourself: What is sticking out? And from what surface is it breaking away? Answer those two questions, and you have understood the sentence perfectly.
9378:
"Jut out" means to stick out or extend beyond a surface or edge — further than the things around it.

Think of a shelf on a wall. If the shelf sticks out into the room, it juts out. The shelf is not flat against the wall. It pushes forward, away from the wall, into the space in front of it.

That's the heart of the phrase: something goes beyond its surroundings. It doesn't stay flat, level, or in line with the rest. It pushes outward.
Breaking the Phrase Apart

"Jut out" is a phrasal verb — a verb ("jut") combined with a particle ("out") that together carry one meaning.

The word "jut" on its own already means to protrude. The word "out" strengthens and clarifies the direction — it emphasizes that something is moving outward, away from a surface or a line. Together, "jut out" is the natural, complete way English speakers use this idea.
Visualizing It

Here are three mental pictures that will lock the meaning in your mind forever:

Picture 1 — A cliff
Imagine you are standing at the edge of a mountain. One part of the rock goes further outward than the rest — it extends into the air over the valley below. That rock formation juts out over the valley.

Picture 2 — A person's chin
Some people have a chin that sticks forward, beyond their lips and nose. That chin juts out. It is more forward than the rest of their face.

Picture 3 — A nail in a wall
A nail that is not fully hammered in juts out from the wall. It is not flat. It extends beyond the surface.

In every picture, the same thing is happening: something extends past its surroundings into open space.
How to Use It in a Sentence

"Jut out" works in several grammatical patterns:

Pattern 1 — Something juts out

The balcony juts out from the building.
A sharp rock juts out of the ground.
His elbow was jutting out and blocking the aisle.

Pattern 2 — Something juts out + direction word
You can add words like from, over, into, above, or beyond to show direction or location:

The branch juts out over the river.
A small peninsula juts out into the sea.
The ledge juts out from the cliff face.

Pattern 3 — Describing an action over time
Since "jut out" is sometimes used to describe a continuous or ongoing state, you will often see it in the continuous form (jutting out):

There was a nail jutting out of the wooden plank.
I could see a rock jutting out from under the snow.
The Feeling the Phrase Carries

"Jut out" often suggests something that is sharp, angular, or unexpected — something that catches your attention because it extends beyond what is around it. It is not a gentle, smooth curve. It tends to imply a somewhat abrupt or definite extension outward.

For example, you would naturally say someone's cheekbones jut out if they are very prominent and sharp — not if their face is soft and round. You would say a rocky headland juts out into the sea — not a gently sloping beach.

This is a subtle quality of the phrase. It suggests something assertive, prominent, or angular in how it extends.
Similar Words and Phrases (Synonyms)

Knowing related words will help you understand "jut out" more deeply and also help you vary your language:

Protrude — the most formal and direct synonym. The pipe protruded from the wall. (More commonly used in technical or formal writing.)

Stick out — very common in everyday speech. A nail is sticking out of that plank. ("Stick out" is more informal and widely used than "jut out.")

Project — used especially in architecture and formal writing. The roof projects outward by two feet.

Overhang — specifically means to jut out above something else, hanging over it. The roof overhangs the porch. ("Overhang" specifically suggests something above, while "jut out" is more general.)

Extend — more neutral and general, without the sharp or angular feeling. The pier extends into the water.

Protrude and stick out are the closest synonyms to "jut out" in most contexts. The key difference is tone: jut out and protrude sound slightly more visual and vivid, while stick out is the most casual.
Opposite Meaning (Antonyms)

The opposite of "jut out" would be described with phrases like:

  • Recede — to go back or inward.
  • Sink in — to go into a surface, rather than out of it.
  • Be flush with — to be perfectly level and flat with a surface, with nothing sticking out.

The door handle is flush with the surface — nothing juts out.
Common Collocations (What "Juts Out" is Used With)

In real-world English, certain nouns appear very often with "jut out." Knowing these will help you recognize and use the phrase naturally:

Physical geography:
Cliffs, rocks, ledges, peninsulas, headlands, and promontories all commonly "jut out."

A rugged headland juts out into the Atlantic.

Architecture and structures:
Balconies, beams, cornices, eaves, roofs, and platforms.

The balcony juts out from the second floor.

The human body:
Chin, jaw, cheekbones, elbows, collarbones, teeth.

His jaw juts out slightly when he is being stubborn.

Objects:
Nails, wires, branches, poles, handles, shelves.

Be careful — there's a wire jutting out from that socket.
Word Forms

You will encounter "jut out" in several forms. Here they are so nothing surprises you:

Base form: jut out → The rocks jut out from the shore.
Past tense: jutted out → A beam jutted out from the ceiling.
Present participle: jutting out → There was a nail jutting out of the wall.
Noun form: a jut (less common; used to refer to the protruding part itself) → There was a small jut of rock above the cave entrance.
Adjective form: jutting → He had a jutting chin. (Here, "jutting" acts as an adjective describing the chin.)
A Few Real-World Example Sentences (in Context)

Here are natural, realistic sentences that show "jut out" working in full context:

The old pier juts out about forty metres into the bay, and fishermen gather there every morning.

She scraped her arm on a nail that was jutting out from the fence.

From the map, you can see how the peninsula juts out dramatically into the Mediterranean Sea.

The new extension of the building juts out awkwardly from the original structure, and many people find it ugly.

His collar bone jutted out visibly — he had lost a great deal of weight.

A single dark rock jutted out above the surface of the water, like a warning.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Jut out" = to extend, stick out, or protrude beyond a surface or the things around it, often in a way that is sharp, prominent, or angular.

It is used for physical objects — geographic features, body parts, structures, and everyday objects — when they extend outward into space beyond their surroundings.

If something is flat and flush with everything around it, it does not jut out. But the moment it pushes forward, sticks outward, or extends beyond the line of the surface it belongs to — it juts out.
9379:
The word juvenile essentially means "of, relating to, or suited to young people" — specifically children and teenagers. Think of it as a more formal, precise way of saying "young" or "youth-related."

But here's what makes this word interesting: it has two distinct uses — one that is completely neutral, and one that carries a negative judgment. Understanding this split is the key to truly knowing the word.
Sense 1: Neutral — Simply "Relating to Young People"

In this sense, juvenile is a purely factual, descriptive word. It has no positive or negative charge. It simply classifies something as belonging to, or designed for, the category of young people (generally under 18).

Examples:

  • A juvenile court — a court specifically designed to handle cases involving minors.
  • A juvenile offender — a young person who has broken the law.
  • Juvenile fiction — books written for children or teens.
  • A juvenile detention center — a facility where young offenders are held.
  • Juvenile diabetes — a form of diabetes that typically first appears in childhood.

In all of these, the word carries zero emotional weight. A doctor saying "juvenile diabetes" is simply naming a category, not making a remark about maturity. A judge saying "juvenile court" is referring to a legal system, not insulting anyone.
Sense 2: Critical — Childish or Immature (in a Negative Way)

This is where the word gains an edge. When used to describe a person's behavior, attitude, humor, or thinking, juvenile means immature and silly in a way that is embarrassing or inappropriate for someone of that age.

The implication here is: "You are acting far younger than you are, and it reflects poorly on you."

Examples:

  • "His response to criticism was completely juvenile — he just started mocking their appearance."
  • "That kind of juvenile humor might get laughs in middle school, but not in a professional meeting."
  • "Stop being so juvenile and have a serious conversation for once."

Notice the pattern: the person being called juvenile is typically not actually young. The word is being used precisely because there is a mismatch — an adult or older teen behaving in a way that is beneath their age. That gap between their actual age and their behavior is what makes the word feel critical and often insulting.

Both senses grow from the same root idea — youth. The first sense uses it factually: This thing belongs to the world of young people. The second sense uses it as a comparison: This behavior belongs to the world of young people, and you shouldn't be displaying it.

A simple way to keep them straight:

  • If juvenile describes a system, institution, or medical condition, it is neutral and factual.
  • If juvenile describes a person's behavior, joke, attitude, or reaction, it is almost always critical.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

In everyday speech, juvenile (especially in Sense 2) tends to sound more formal and sharper than simply saying "childish." When someone calls your behavior childish, it feels like a mild rebuke. When they call it juvenile, it sounds more deliberate and cutting — like a considered judgment, not just an offhand remark. This is why you'll often see it in written criticism, formal complaints, or moments when someone is firmly putting another person down.

• Childish — Very similar to Sense 2, but softer and more commonly used in casual speech.
  • Immature — Focuses more on emotional or psychological underdevelopment; broader than juvenile.
  • Puerile — Almost identical in meaning to Sense 2, but far more formal and literary; rarely used in everyday speech.
  • Adolescent — Can be used similarly to juvenile in Sense 2, but more specifically evokes teenage-style drama or rebellion.

Juvenile sits between childish (mild, casual) and puerile (very formal, literary) in terms of formality and sharpness.

• Mature — The most direct opposite in Sense 2.
  • Adult — Opposing in both senses.
  • Sophisticated — Especially in the context of humor or attitude.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

Sense 1Factual. Means "related to young people." No judgment. (juvenile court, juvenile offender)
Sense 2Critical. Means "immature and silly in a way unbefitting one's age." (juvenile behavior, juvenile humor)

The word is always connected to youth — either describing something that genuinely belongs to youth, or accusing someone of behaving as though they belong there when they shouldn't.
